caveats: Storage on-site: county overlaps the Mt. Simon Sandstone saline storage formation.

ranked.label: BECCS pulp & paper
pros: Retrofits an existing pulp & paper mill — low execution risk, near-term

Leverages existing biomass logistics + grid connection
Proximate geologic storage here
cons: Requires an existing mill to retrofit
Capture capex on flue gas

ranked.label: Biomass burial
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Simple and low-cost; needs no geologic CO2 storage
Works for distributed biomass
Removes carbon and nutrients from an over-fertilized landscape
cons: Durability still being validated (Frontier prepurchase, not offtake)
No emissions-avoiding co-product; nutrient-export risk with ag residues

ranked.label: BECCS (heat/electricity)
pros: High CDR efficiency (~80%)
Energy co-product (heat/electricity) displaces fossil emissions
Low durability risk; Frontier's most-preferred pathway

cons: Capital-intensive; works best at large scale
Not very modular — hard to deploy in distributed settings

Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes

Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here

caveats: Storage on-site: county overlaps the Mt. Simon Sandstone saline storage formation.

ranked.label: BECCS (heat/electricity)
pros: High CDR efficiency (~80%)
Energy co-product (heat/electricity) displaces fossil emissions
Low durability risk; Frontier's most-preferred pathway
Proximate geologic storage here
cons: Capital-intensive; works best at large scale
Not very modular — hard to deploy in distributed settings

ranked.label: Biomass burial
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Simple and low-cost; needs no geologic CO2 storage
Works for distributed biomass
Removes carbon and nutrients from an over-fertilized landscape
cons: Durability still being validated (Frontier prepurchase, not offtake)
No emissions-avoiding co-product; nutrient-export risk with ag residues

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
Proximate geologic storage here
cons: No emissions-avoiding co-product
Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far

ranked.label: Bio-oil (pyrolysis)
pros: Modular and distributed (Charm-style roving model)

Low durability risk
cons: Lower CDR efficiency (~45%)
Needs dry/solid biomass — not for wet feedstocks
Higher $/t than injection where storage is proximate
Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here

rationale: Concentrated dry agricultural residues, excess nutrient status, good geologic storage access (nearest qualifying storage ~0 km) with a retrofittable pulp_paper anchor (Domtar Paper Co Llc Hawesville Mill) -> BECCS retrofit of existing pulp & paper / bioenergy maximizes CDR efficiency (80%) plus energy co-product -- Frontier's top-preferred use of biomass.
caveats: Storage on-site: county overlaps the Mt. Simon Sandstone saline storage formation.

ranked.label: BECCS pulp & paper
pros: Retrofits an existing pulp & paper mill — low execution risk, near-term
High CDR efficiency (~80%) from concentrated recovery-boiler flue gas
Leverages existing biomass logistics + grid connection
Proximate geologic storage here
cons: Requires an existing mill to retrofit
Capture capex on flue gas

ranked.label: Biomass burial
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Simple and low-cost; needs no geologic CO2 storage
Works for distributed biomass
Removes carbon and nutrients from an over-fertilized landscape
cons: Durability still being validated (Frontier prepurchase, not offtake)
No emissions-avoiding co-product; nutrient-export risk with ag residues

ranked.label: BECCS (heat/electricity)
pros: High CDR efficiency (~80%)
Energy co-product (heat/electricity) displaces fossil emissions
Low durability risk; Frontier's most-preferred pathway
Proximate geologic storage here
cons: Capital-intensive; works best at large scale
Not very modular — hard to deploy in distributed settings

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
Proximate geologic storage here
cons: No emissions-avoiding co-product
Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far

ranked.label: Bio-oil (pyrolysis)
pros: Modular and distributed (Charm-style roving model)
Pyrolysis densifies the carbon, so it is cheap to haul to distant wells

Needs dry/solid biomass — not for wet feedstocks
Higher $/t than injection where storage is proximate
Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here

caveats: Storage on-site: county overlaps the Basal Sands - Rome Trough saline storage formation.

ranked.label: BECCS (heat/electricity)
pros: High CDR efficiency (~80%)
Energy co-product (heat/electricity) displaces fossil emissions
Low durability risk; Frontier's most-preferred pathway
cons: Capital-intensive; works best at large scale
Not very modular — hard to deploy in distributed settings
Transport to the nearest operating well is costly (~$98/tCO₂)
Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost

ranked.label: Bio-oil (pyrolysis)
pros: Modular and distributed (Charm-style roving model)
Pyrolysis densifies the carbon, so it is cheap to haul to distant wells
Returns biochar and nutrients to fields
Low durability risk
cons: Lower CDR efficiency (~45%)
Needs dry/solid biomass — not for wet feedstocks
Higher $/t than injection where storage is proximate

ranked.label: Biomass burial
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Simple and low-cost; needs no geologic CO2 storage
Works for distributed biomass
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Durability still being validated (Frontier prepurchase, not offtake)
No emissions-avoiding co-product; nutrient-export risk with ag residues

ranked.label: Biochar
pros: Returns nutrients to soils, improving yields
Distributed and storage-independent; simple and near-term
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Low CDR efficiency (~30%)
Durability and verification questions; Frontier's lower-preference pathway

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$146/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here

Low durability risk

name: Columbiana

storage_detail.nearest_well: Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations

rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, excess nutrient status, moderate geologic storage access (~0 km) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~50% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest operating well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.
Storage on-site: county overlaps the Bass Island Dolomite saline storage formation.

ranked.label: Bio-oil (hydrothermal liquefaction)
pros: Handles WET biomass (manure/biosolids) directly — no drying needed
Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)
Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
Removes carbon and nutrients from an over-fertilized landscape
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$135/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here
No emissions-avoiding co-product
Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far
Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost
